proposals.name: Skyport Station
proposals.type: Airship Port, Rail Exchange & Civic Order Facility
proposals.entry:
Type: Airship Port, Rail Exchange & Civic Order Facility
Location: Between Heliot Station and the Circus grounds
Common Names: Skyport, the Tower
Controlled By: Civic Order
Connected To: Heliot Station and Fogport's elevated rail network

Skyport Station is Fogport's great port in the sky: a towering iron structure of girders, platforms, lifts, cranes, advertisements and airship berths rising above the neighborhoods between Heliot Station and the Circus.

It is considerably newer than Heliot Station and considerably less beautiful.

Where Heliot was built to impress arriving travelers with stonework, vaulted glass and civic grandeur, Skyport was built quickly and vertically. Its enormous iron frame resembles a factory chimney crossed with a railway trestle. Platforms have been added, removed and extended repeatedly as aerial commerce increased.

From a distance, docked zeppelins appear to hang from the tower like strange fruit.

Skyport has become one of the defining structures of eastern Fogport. Together, Heliot and Skyport make the surrounding district the city's principal transportation interchange: ships below, trains and trams through Heliot, and international air traffic overhead.

The Airship Berths

The upper-middle levels contain Skyport's commercial berths.

Steam-powered zeppelins arrive from across the Hundred Kingdoms carrying passengers, machinery, luxury goods, diplomatic cargo and anything valuable enough to justify moving it through the air.

Because many of those kingdoms are presently at war with one another, international airships are deliberately distinctive. Hull colors, tail configurations, national crests and enormous painted insignia allow an approaching vessel to be identified long before anyone can read its registration.

Mistaking one nation's airship for another can be considerably more serious than a clerical error.

Docking arms extend outward from the tower. Passengers disembark onto narrow enclosed galleries while cargo is transferred by cranes onto freight platforms. Heavy containers can be lowered directly to the rail levels below.

Customs officers maintain inspection rooms throughout these levels, although experienced merchants know that the thoroughness of an inspection varies considerably according to the inspector, cargo and accompanying envelope.

The Heliot Connection

Skyport was deliberately constructed beside the existing Heliot rail approaches.

Several elevated tracks branch from the Heliot lines and pass directly beneath and through Skyport. Passenger lifts descend from the airship galleries to the rail platforms, while freight elevators and cranes allow imported cargo to be transferred directly onto trains.

This arrangement has transformed the neighborhood into a perpetual traffic knot.

Locals complain about the noise. Merchants complain whenever it stops.

The Advertising Faces

The lower and middle tower are covered in enormous vertical advertisements facing different parts of Fogport.

Wine merchants, perfume houses, restaurants, theaters and luxury manufacturers compete fiercely for the largest spaces. Different faces of the tower have developed distinct palettes of painted boards, illuminated signs, mechanical displays and hanging banners.

One advertisement dwarfs all the others.

A huge black-and-red stencil portrait of First Citizen Vaunt Quell, unmistakable by his metal jaw, looks across the city beneath the words: BEHOLD FOGPORT.

Depending upon where one stands, Vaunt appears to be watching the railway, the Circus, Heliot Station or the neighborhoods below.

Fogporters have consequently developed numerous obscene names for the advertisement. None are printed here.

The Crown

The highest portion of Skyport does not belong to the commercial port.

Above the international berths, ordinary stairways simply stop. Gates marked CIVIC VIGILANCE — RESTRICTED block further ascent.

The upper tower contains signal equipment, observation galleries, communications rooms, armories and a permanent Civic Vigilance detachment. From here the Order has an extraordinary view of the eastern city, Heliot approaches and much of the harbor.

More importantly, the Crown maintains its own small aerial fleet.

Maton Rapid Deployment

The small red airships circling Skyport are not taxis.

They are identical Civic Vigilance deployment craft: compact propeller-driven zeppelins bearing the Civic eye insignia. Each carries a small crew and several Civic Order Patrolmatons — C.O.P.s, better known on the street as Patrolmatons, Tinners, or simply Cops.

Their purpose is brutally straightforward.

When Civic Vigilance requires mechanical officers somewhere quickly, a deployment craft leaves the Crown, crosses the city above rooftops and lowers its Patrolmatons close to the disturbance.

The extraordinarily long arms and legs of the Tinners make watching several of them descend from an airship particularly unpleasant.

Older Fogporters still find this remarkable. Younger Fogporters simply look upward whenever someone shouts: “Cops!”

A Foreign Machine

Skyport is also inseparable from Fogport's increasing dependence on foreign technology.

The Patrolmatons themselves are imported from one of the Hundred Kingdoms rather than manufactured in Fogport. Replacement mechanisms, specialized tools and occasionally entire new machines arrive through Skyport.

This creates an uncomfortable irony that critics of the Civic Order enjoy pointing out: Some of the government's most loyal officers are foreign imports.

They are loyal precisely because they have nowhere else to belong.

GM Secrets

The Fifteen-Year Reform

The introduction of Patrolmatons followed a serious internal crisis within Civic Vigilance roughly fifteen years ago.

The official history describes the incident as an administrative reorganization. It was considerably worse.

A substantial number of human Vigilance officers refused orders during a confrontation that threatened to turn parts of Fogport against the Civic Order. Some deserted. Some sided with civilians. Others simply disappeared.

Vaunt's government learned an important lesson: Human officers can decide not to obey.

The first large shipment of Patrolmatons arrived through Skyport soon afterward. Cost savings were emphasized publicly. Loyalty was the real reason.

The Sealed Berth

One of the original upper freight platforms has been closed for years. Officially, its structure is unsafe.

Inside are shipping crates from the earliest Maton deliveries. Some are empty. Some are not.

Several contain models that were rejected before deployment, including experimental machines whose instructions and identification plates are written entirely in the language of their manufacturer.

Civic engineers have never successfully activated them.

Recently, one crate was discovered open.

Neutral Ground in the Sky

Fogport's neutrality makes Skyport extremely valuable during the War of the Hundred Kingdoms.

Airships belonging to nations actively fighting one another sometimes occupy neighboring berths.

The Civic Order enforces an absolute prohibition against foreign hostilities within Skyport.

This has created one of the strangest places in Fogport: enemy officers drinking in the same elevated waiting rooms while their crews glare at one another through glass walls.

Spies adore Skyport.

The Cargo Problem

Air freight is expensive. Consequently, almost everything arriving through Skyport is important.

Diplomatic correspondence. Prototype machinery. Medicine. Jewelry. Weapons. Lumen apparatus. Rare food. Intelligence documents. Foreign currency. People who do not want their arrival recorded at the docks.

A single incorrectly routed container can therefore become an adventure. And containers are incorrectly routed with surprising frequency.

The Tower Never Sleeps

Skyport operates continuously.

At three in the morning its passenger galleries may be nearly empty, but somewhere above, cables are still moving, engines are turning, customs clerks are stamping papers and enormous shapes are emerging silently from the fog.

There are maintenance ladders running through virtually the entire structure.

There are also places where the original plans no longer correspond to the tower.

Skyport has been modified too many times. Entire platforms exist that no current department admits maintaining.

Adventure Hooks

The Wrong Zeppelin: An airship approaches Skyport displaying the colors and crest of a friendly kingdom. A dockworker who actually served aboard that nation's ships notices that its tail configuration is completely wrong.

Three Tinners Missing: A Civic deployment zeppelin returns to the Crown without three of its Patrolmatons. Nobody aboard can explain where they went.

The Diplomatic Container: A freight container belonging to a foreign embassy is accidentally sent down the Heliot freight line before customs inspection. Several governments immediately begin looking for it.

Dinner Above the Fog: Byl and Lott are invited to an expensive Skyport restaurant overlooking the airship berths. Their host never arrives. His hat does.

The Unscheduled Arrival: In the middle of the night, an enormous foreign zeppelin emerges from the fog without signal lamps, national colors or a requested berth. Skyport signals it repeatedly. The airship does not answer. But it continues approaching.
